description: I Am The Cavalry talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: Hackers Kinda Like to Eat
talks.teaser: Covers cyber risks to water, farm and hospital systems, from ransomware on utilities to exposed industrial controllers.
talks.summary:
The session argues that food supply depends on water, power, farm technology and hospitals, and that all of them are becoming more internet-connected. The two presenters, one from an incident response firm and one from a life sciences information sharing group, open with a 2023 ransomware attack on a UK water company that served over a million people. The attackers shifted toward data extortion, and their claims of reaching operational systems were never confirmed.

They then describe a 2023 campaign by a state-linked group that reached about ten US water facilities through internet-exposed industrial controllers protected by weak or default passwords. The group defaced the devices with political messages instead of disrupting service. Remotely operated center pivot irrigation systems were presented as a similar exposure, and nitrate contamination was used to show how an upset in water quality can strain hospitals. The talk also raised the possibility that a conflict could disrupt ports, cold storage and power, with Russian wiper attacks in Ukraine as a reference point.

For practitioners, the advice centers on removing industrial devices from the internet, separating operational networks from IT, changing default credentials, and keeping an accurate asset inventory that includes forgotten systems. Organizations should keep incident response contacts and out-of-band communication current, rehearse with tabletop exercises, maintain manual fallbacks, and share indicators through sector groups. The closing section moved to household preparedness, covering food and water stockpiles, local production, neighbour networks and paper maps.

talks.title: Time is Running Out - Tying it All Together - What Will You Do in the Near Term?
talks.teaser: Makes the case for short-term steps to protect water, hospitals and emergency care from cyber disruption.
talks.summary:
This closing session for the I Am the Cavalry track has Josh Corman recap the first year of the Undisruptible 27 pilot. He screens two short draft videos that use storytelling to show how attacks on hospitals and water systems could cut off patient care and endanger lives, not just expose records. Reactions were split: some viewers found the material too frightening, others said it was not frightening enough, which shaped how the messaging will be tailored to utility operators, city officials and emergency managers.

Corman explains what the pilot learned. Building trust with water engineers helped identify plausible physical harms, such as pressure shocks in aging pipes, and pointed toward practical fixes. A central idea is consequence-informed engineering: when a pump or ventilator fails, restoring from backups is too slow, so the priority is to prevent or absorb the hit. He gives a low-cost example, an analog pressure switch that shuts off a pump independently of networked controls. The next two-year plan targets about a dozen communities where water systems and hospitals depend on each other, with lessons meant to spread to the wider set of hospital-linked systems.

He closes by asking attendees to nominate communities, join the project's Slack, and volunteer through the cyber resilience corps. The takeaway is that concrete, near-term measures matter more than waiting for long-range policy, and that practitioners can help local leaders act before the next disruption.

talks.title: Defending Our Water - Defending Our Lives
talks.teaser: Panel on applying engineering principles to limit cyber attack impacts on US water and wastewater systems.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the scale of the US water sector, which spans roughly 150,000 systems from large metropolitan utilities to small local operators. The speakers say cyber risk has climbed the list of utility concerns, while regulation remains uneven, with state rules varying and a proposed federal water body still pending. They frame the core problem as a gap between IT teams that manage the digital layer and engineers who understand which physical processes can fail.

The middle of the session introduces cyber-informed engineering, a method that asks engineers to identify the worst consequences an adversary could cause and to design process safeguards that limit them, rather than relying only on perimeter defense. The speakers stress that digitally enabled failure modes can damage equipment even when a system appears to run faster or smoother. They describe assessments where utilities now discuss worst-day scenarios more openly than before. A worked example of a booster pump station with cloud-based control shows how a low-cost time-delay relay and a pressure tank could keep an attacker from damaging pumps, turning a severe threat into a recoverable outage.

The closing segment covers adoption. Cost concerns are answered by prioritizing high-consequence assets and piloting narrowly, and state grant scoring that rewards engineering-based cyber planning is offered as an example of incentives. Exercises that run operators through a day without SCADA are presented as a practical starting point. The takeaways are to involve engineers and operators early, build on existing safety and reliability practices, and encourage community members to engage with their local utility and council.

talks.title: Power Play: AI Dominance Depends on Energy Resilience
talks.teaser: Examines how AI data-center growth strains the electric grid and why energy resilience matters for AI.
talks.summary:
Presented in the I Am The Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas 2025, this talk argues that AI growth and the electric grid can no longer be treated separately. The speakers describe a cycle in which AI systems depend on power and cooling, while utilities increasingly lean on AI for their own operations. They contrast a grid being built around large data-center loads with one that already struggles to serve ordinary customers reliably.

The middle section explains why large loads matter. Grid operators keep generation and demand in balance to hold frequency steady, and AI training can cause sudden swings of roughly 15 megawatts at a single site. The speakers cited about 200 near-miss events in which data centers disconnected without warning, and a lightning-related fault in Northern Virginia that prompted dozens of facilities to switch to backup generation at once, abruptly removing a large block of load. Small rural cooperatives, often where these sites are being built, have limited cyber staff and planning models that do not yet account for data-center behavior.

The closing part turns to practical responses: demand transparency from data-center operators, consequence-based planning, chaos-style testing of assumptions, and black-start plans that include data centers. The speakers noted that restoration tools relying on data centers could push hospitals further down the queue. Their central point was that planning for failure and recovering quickly matters as much as prevention, with the Iberian Peninsula outage cited as a case where a prepared restart worked.

talks.title: Setting the Table - WarGames 2027 & Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs as Hybrid Warfare Nears
talks.teaser: Frames dependence on water, power and hospitals as a growing hybrid-warfare risk ahead of 2027.
talks.summary:
The opening session of the I Am The Cavalry track frames the next two and a half days of talks. Josh Corman traces the track's origins to 2013, when hacker volunteers began offering public-safety advice to government, and introduces the Undisruptible 2027 project. Its core idea is to protect a short list of lifeline functions, such as water, emergency care and power, that people cannot go without for long.

Much of the session is an interactive exercise in which the audience ranks priorities, such as patient privacy against timely treatment. The speakers argue that ransomware on hospitals can cause measurable deaths, and they use a water main failure as an example of physical consequences. They point to state-linked groups such as Volt Typhoon and note that most lifeline infrastructure is privately owned, that cyber insurance often excludes acts of war, and that federal defensive support has shrunk. Bryson Bort adds a national security view, arguing that the threat is a combination of motive, capability and access, and that engineering limits on consequences matter as much as preventing intrusion.

The practical takeaway is to plan for disruption rather than assume prevention will hold. Attendees are encouraged to learn about consequence-informed engineering, to engage local water, hospital and emergency managers, and to think about how their own households would cope if services failed.

talks.title: Cyber Civil Defense: Volunteers to the Rescue
talks.teaser: Maps US cyber volunteering programs that help under-resourced organizations and proposes short- and long-term steps to scale them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the gap in cybersecurity help for organizations that deliver essential public services, such as municipalities, hospitals, school districts and nonprofits. These groups often cannot afford protection or hire staff with the right skills. The speaker, a policy researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Long-Term Cyber Security, explains how her team spent six months mapping existing volunteer efforts with about thirty experts from insurance, consulting, academia, and managed service providers.

The landscape falls into three groups: state-run civilian cyber corps, university clinics, and nonprofit-led volunteer groups. Their services include incident response, risk assessments, training, and threat intelligence sharing. Access is uneven, many organizations do not know these programs exist, and liability agreements, volatile funding, and inconsistent impact metrics limit their growth. The roadmap recommends near-term steps such as expanding programs into underserved states, clarifying liability protections, improving volunteer-to-client matching, and giving organizations handoff resources and guidance for choosing managed providers. Longer-term ideas include secure-by-default products, state-backed shared service pools for utilities, and security education in schools.

The main takeaway for attendees is to find a local volunteer program and to press policymakers to fund state-level programs. The speaker pointed to the roadmap, a state guidebook with model bills, and an upcoming conference session on the volunteer distribution networks.

talks.title: End of Life (EOL) Equipment should not mean End of Life (Your Life)
talks.teaser: Examines how end-of-life routers, smart devices and industrial gear leave unpatched risks threatening public safety.
talks.summary:
This I Am The Cavalry panel, with Stacey Higginbotham, Silas Cutler and Paul Roberts, looks at equipment that has reached end of support but stays connected and in service. The opening frames the problem with consumer data on smart devices that owners never learn are unsupported, and with home and small office routers that number in the tens of millions and often carry known flaws. The speakers tie these devices to state-linked intrusion campaigns and to botnets that use them as relay infrastructure.

The middle of the talk moves from the home into enterprise and operational technology. It describes a botnet built on end-of-life routers and cameras, and how a takedown can still leave devices exposed to reinfection. It also covers a vendor VPN appliance whose firmware was found to run an unsupported operating system, an old Linux kernel and outdated libraries carrying many known vulnerabilities. Industrial operators, by contrast, typically plan for obsolescence over decades, and the speakers suggest that planning habit could carry over to other sectors.

The closing section turns to policy and practice. Proposals include minimum support periods printed on product labels, advance notice before support ends, software bills of materials, and graceful handoffs such as escrow or open-sourcing. For practitioners, the talk recommends inventorying devices, writing an end-of-life plan, rehearsing offline operations, and asking whether a product can run software other than the vendor's own.

talks.title: A Month Without External Assistance
talks.teaser: Explains how households and neighborhoods can plan to go 30 days without outside help.
talks.summary:
The session poses a thought experiment: could a household and its neighborhood sustain themselves for 30 days without outside help? The speaker sets aside extreme survivalist prepping and frames the question around community, asking attendees to consider who lives nearby, including elderly, disabled, or transportation-limited neighbors, and what skills those people may bring.

The middle of the talk moves into practical steps. Neighborhood hazards such as wildfire, flooding, evacuation routes and local crime should be identified with help from local officials and then ranked by risk. At the household level the speaker covers low-cost basics like batteries, tools, small bills, hygiene items, copies of vital records and basic medical supplies. Water planning ranges from commercial containers and reused soda bottles to boiling, chlorination and distillation, based on roughly a gallon per person per day. Food should be shelf-stable, low-prep, stored against pests and rotated.

The talk closes by treating preparedness as a months-long project rather than a single weekend task. Attendees left with homework: map local risks, check whether schools and employers have tested their plans, and talk with neighbors. In questions, an audience member raised the difficulty lower-income households face. An emergency manager suggested focusing on inventorying skills and needs rather than gathering supplies, and pointed to community emergency response teams and local hazard mitigation plans.

talks.title: Emergency & Urgent Care Remains in Critical Condition
talks.teaser: Panel examines how ransomware and outages disrupt hospital care, and what practical and policy responses could help.
talks.summary:
The session opened with a short video on how ransomware at hospitals can delay time-sensitive care, even at facilities that were never attacked. Beau Woods drew on his years doing IT security inside a hospital to describe legacy medical devices that reacted badly to routine network traffic, antivirus that shut down a vendor's clinical application, and login delays that cost emergency staff precious minutes. He also recounted restoring fetal monitors during a worm outbreak after leadership approved the fix, showing how approvals can come when the patient-safety stakes are laid out plainly.

Dina Carlisle, a critical care nurse and union president, described weeks of downtime at two hospital systems. Staff fell back to paper charting, the pharmacy safety net for medication checks disappeared, lab results were missing before surgeries, and newer clinicians had little experience writing orders by hand. She argued for enforceable staffing ratios and contract language that requires communication and training during outages. Christian Dameff presented research from his academic healthcare security center, linking ransomware in one health system to longer emergency waits, diversion at neighboring hospitals, and worse cardiac arrest outcomes. He also described a CrowdStrike outage that disrupted hundreds of hospitals' services, and a prototype called Crash Cart that restores a 20-bed emergency department's core IT from a vehicle using private cellular networks and satellite backhaul.

Audience questions covered state staffing legislation, whether HIPAA shapes contingency planning, scaling portable systems, and recovering data for electronic health records. The panel's takeaways were that prevention alone will not cover response, that organizations need to map the critical third-party vendors they depend on, and that clinicians and communities must press for accountability.

talks.title: Ransomware As Canary For Societal Disruption
talks.teaser: Argues that ransomware already disrupts essential services as much as state attacks, and that shared controls can address both.
talks.summary:
Joe Slowik argues that ransomware is already causing the kind of disruption to hospitals, schools and other essential services that policymakers usually link to future state-directed attacks. He points to the Düsseldorf case, where an ambulance was rerouted after an attack and patient care suffered, and notes that wiper-style incidents have often done more real damage than the speculative operational technology attacks that draw most of the attention.

The middle of the talk compares the tradecraft of ransomware affiliates with that of state groups such as Volt Typhoon. Both tend to rely on stolen credentials, weak or missing multi-factor authentication, exposed edge devices and living-off-the-land techniques. Drawing on ATT&CK data, threat reports and incident analyses, he argues that this overlap means one set of controls can address both kinds of adversary. Examples include enforcing multi-factor authentication on external services, reducing exposed attack surface, improving vulnerability management and limiting administrative movement.

He closes by urging communicators to frame threats around immediate, tangible operational impact rather than distant scenarios, which may make it easier for asset owners to justify investment. He also acknowledges limits: many under-resourced organizations cannot implement these controls, so residual risk remains. Business continuity, disaster recovery and the ability to rebuild systems quickly are presented as necessary additions. In the Q&A, the discussion touched on the ecosystem of access brokers and affiliates and the value of detailed, actionable incident reporting.

talks.title: Cyber Incident Command System (CICS): A people orchestration layer
talks.teaser: Applies the national incident management command structure to cyber incidents, covering roles, staff safety and span of control.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem in incident response: a small group of people ends up solving the problem and cannot rest, hand off work or easily bring in replacements. That strains staff, and fatigue leads to mistakes that make incidents worse. The speakers propose a lighter version of the National Incident Management System, the command standard that emergency responders already use across the United States, adapted for cyber and IT teams.

The middle of the talk focuses on command and control. It covers modular organization and manageable span of control, with supervisors overseeing three to seven people and five as the preferred number. The structure separates an incident commander from operations, planning, logistics, and finance and administration, and adds roles such as a public information officer, a legal officer and a mental health officer. A hospital ransomware example shows the structure growing as the incident does, with existing technical playbooks plugging into the IT operations section unchanged and medical teams added as another operations branch. A tabletop exercise with public health officials is described as showing that people from different organizations quickly settled on this structure.

The question period raised concerns about staffing shortages, uninvited volunteers, corporate reluctance to add mental health roles and whether companies would accept work-rest limits. The speakers suggested taking the roles and work-rest ratios from wildfire guidance, using free federal training, and running exercises to show leadership who needs to be involved. The main takeaway is to define roles and shift limits before an incident so that outside responders can join using a shared structure.

talks.title: Can You Hear Me Now? A Survey of Communications Platforms During Emergencies
talks.teaser: Surveys licensed and unlicensed radio options, from CB and GMRS to amateur radio and Meshtastic, for communicating during emergencies.
talks.summary:
Slava opens with a practical question: when roads are blocked and normal infrastructure is down, how does an individual reach family miles away and coordinate with others? He frames radio as a frequency range combined with a modulation scheme, then uses that lens to compare the services available to private citizens in the United States.

The middle of the talk covers Citizens Band, Family Radio Service, General Mobile Radio Service and amateur radio. For each, he goes through licensing cost and effort, power limits, channel counts and typical range. He notes that CB can sometimes travel far through atmospheric propagation, while FRS and GMRS are mostly line of sight. He then turns to LoRa and Meshtastic, a low-cost mesh platform on ESP32-class hardware. The key security point is that encryption is permitted under the unlicensed Part 15 rules but prohibited under amateur Part 97, so an operator must choose between identifying with a call sign and using encrypted channels. He also demonstrates telemetry, GPIO control of remote hardware and MQTT bridging, and notes that crowded default channels saturate at large events.

He closes with practical advice. Antenna quality and height usually matter more than transmitter power, a station must be able to receive as well as send, and people should identify their likely risks and prepare before an emergency. The audience questions covered legal gray areas, node triangulation and power limits.

talks.title: Cascading Failure, Unified Defense: Defending Water, Power, Healthcare, & EMS
talks.teaser: Shows how attacks on water and power systems cascade into hospital and EMS failures, and how joint planning can help.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a walk-through of a cardiac patient in an ambulance whose route to the nearest hospital is diverted after a water utility is hit by a cyberattack. Hospitals lose water pressure, sterilization, dialysis and cooling, and the golden hour slips away. The speakers, who draw on first-responder and security experience, frame this as a chain where a weak link in one utility can disable care far from the original target.

Next they describe state-linked groups such as Volt Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, which they say persist for years by abusing edge devices like VPNs and firewalls, blending traffic into legitimate cloud services, and rotating command channels. They also cover how dispatch centers can fall back to paper maps when geocoding fails, and why legacy OT systems that cannot be patched are hard to retire.

The closing section gives practical guidance: prioritize patching internet-facing devices using CISA's KEV list, enforce MFA, segment IT from OT, centralize logs, and test restores. It also recommends joint playbooks that merge cyber and emergency-management plans, regional mutual aid, cross-training through free courses, sector ISACs, and community steps such as CPR training and volunteering.
